title: Making predictions from a text
blurb: Predict what is most likely to happen next by following the patterns, traits, trends and causes the text has already set in motion.
question: A TEAS passage says a course's enrollment has risen three years in a row and a hospital will now pay the fees of any employee who enrolls. One answer says enrollment will fall; another says the college will hire three new instructors. What is the best prediction, and why are those two wrong?

teach.h: A prediction is a forecast from evidence
teach.body: Formally, a prediction is a judgment about what is likely to happen next, or in a new situation, based on patterns, character traits, causes already in motion, stated trends and foreshadowing in the text. In plain English: you look at where the text is heading and say what comes next. A good prediction follows from the text, not from hope, fear or what you know from outside it.

teach.caption: Most TEAS prediction items rest on one or two of these clues.

teach.body: (1) Enrollment in Lakeside Community College's evening nursing assistant course has risen three years in a row, from 40 students to 55 to 72. (2) The college still has one evening instructor, who teaches every section. (3) This summer, a nearby hospital announced it will pay the course fees of any employee who enrolls. (4) The hospital employs more than 900 support staff.

teach.caption: The trend is rising, and sentence 3 adds a new cause pushing the same way. Nothing in the text pushes it down.

items: Find the direction: what pattern, trend or trait does the text set up? (Enrollment is rising.)
Look for causes still at work: is anything new pushing harder or reversing it? (Paid fees push it higher.)
Choose the outcome that follows most directly: enrollment likely rises again, adding strain on one instructor.
Reject options that need an event the text never mentions, or that reverse the trend with no cause.

teach.caption: Predictions and inferences both need text evidence; an assumption is something the reader brings in.

teach.body: In narratives, character traits are the strongest clue. If a passage shows Elena checking her alarm twice, packing her bag the night before and arriving early to every shift, then when her car will not start, she most likely calls for a ride at once rather than giving up on the day. People in a text keep acting the way the text has shown them acting, unless the text gives a reason for a change.

bands.label: Follows the text's pattern or cause
Needs an event the text never gives
Reverses the trend with no cause

teach.text: Watch for three wrong predictions: one that needs an unstated event ('the college will hire three instructors'), one that reverses the trend without a cause ('enrollment will drop'), and one with absolute language ('every hospital employee will enroll'). The trend supports more students, not all 900 staff.

teach.body: Andre Williams, preparing for an LPN program, reads the Lakeside passage. He rejects 'The college will close the evening course' because nothing points to closure. He rejects 'All 900 hospital employees will enroll' as an overstatement. He chooses 'Enrollment will likely rise again, adding to the evening instructor's workload' because it extends the rising trend, uses the new cause in sentence 3 and connects to the single instructor in sentence 2.

items: A prediction says what is likely next, based only on evidence in the text.
Clues: patterns, character traits, causes in motion, stated trends, foreshadowing.
A trend continues unless the text gives a reason for it to change.
Reject predictions that need an unstated event or use unearned absolutes.
Characters keep acting in character unless the text shows a reason to change.

summary: You can now predict what is most likely to happen next by following the patterns, traits, trends and causes a text sets up. You can also reject predictions that rely on unstated events, reverse a trend without cause or overreach with absolute language.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Mrs. Alvarez has run the school's lost-and-found for twelve years. She labels every item with the date it was found, keeps a written log and phones families whenever a name is written inside a jacket or lunchbox. Today, a student hands her a calculator with 'J. Park, Room 14' scratched on the back.

What will Mrs. Alvarez most likely do next?
options: Place the calculator in the bin and wait for someone to ask.
Log the calculator and contact the Park family or Room 14.
Give the calculator to the student who turned it in to her.
Ask the principal to announce the find over the loudspeaker.
A.why: The passage shows a consistent pattern: she logs items and contacts families when a name is found. The calculator has a name and room, so she will most likely log it and reach the owner.

whyNot.0: This ignores her habit of contacting owners whenever a name is present.
whyNot.2: Nothing in her established routine suggests giving items to finders.
whyNot.3: Announcements are never part of her routine; this needs a new behavior the text does not show.

A.q:
Read the passage.

The Brookfield bus line added a stop outside the new medical center in January. Daily riders at that stop grew from 40 in January to 85 in February and 130 in March. In April, the medical center will open an urgent care wing with evening hours.

Based on the passage, which prediction is most reasonable for the stop after April?
options: Ridership will level off now that the center is fully open.
Ridership will fall as patients choose to drive to the center.
Ridership will keep rising as the new wing draws more visitors.
The bus line will add a second stop at the medical center.
A.why: Ridership has risen each month, and the new urgent care wing adds another reason to visit. Both the trend and a new cause point to further growth.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests the center is already 'fully open'; a new wing is still to come.
whyNot.1: This reverses the trend with no cause given in the text.
whyNot.3: A second stop is an unstated event; the passage gives no plan for it.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Tomas had planned the family picnic for weeks. On Saturday morning he noticed the sky turning a heavy gray, and the radio warned of thunderstorms by noon. His sister texted that the park's covered pavilion was still available to reserve.

Which event is most likely to happen next?
options: Tomas cancels the picnic and tells the family to stay home.
Tomas holds the picnic in the open field as first planned.
Tomas postpones the picnic until the following summer.
Tomas reserves the pavilion and moves the picnic under it.
A.why: The storm warning creates the problem, his weeks of planning show he wants the picnic to happen, and his sister's text supplies a solution. Reserving the pavilion follows from all three clues.

whyNot.0: Canceling ignores the pavilion option the text sets up as the solution.
whyNot.1: Staying in the open field ignores the thunderstorm warning.
whyNot.2: Waiting a year is a large jump with no support; a same-day solution is available.

B.q:
Read the passage.

As Grace unlocked the clinic on her first day as office manager, she noticed the backup generator's warning light blinking. She made a note to call the repair company, then got swept up in the morning rush of patients. At 2 p.m., the weather service issued a storm alert for the evening.

The details about the generator and the storm most likely foreshadow which event?
options: Grace will be promoted for handling her first day so calmly.
The storm will cut the power and the generator will fail.
The repair company will arrive before the morning rush begins.
The clinic will close early so patients can avoid the storm.
B.why: An unfixed warning light on a backup generator, plus an evening storm alert, sets up a likely power failure in which the generator does not work properly. That is classic foreshadowing.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the passage hints at a promotion; the details point to a problem.
whyNot.2: The morning rush has already passed, and Grace never made the call.
whyNot.3: Closing early is possible, but it does not use the generator clue the author planted.

B.q:
Read the passage.

For five years, the town of Millbrook's population grew by about 300 people a year as families moved in for jobs at the Hartwell plant. Last month, Hartwell announced that it will close the plant next year and move all its jobs to another state.

Which prediction about Millbrook's population is best supported?
options: Growth will continue at about 300 new residents per year.
Growth will slow or reverse as plant jobs leave the town.
The town will grow faster as new employers move into it.
The population will double within the next five years.
B.why: The text links the growth to jobs at the plant. With the plant closing, the cause of the trend is ending, so the trend is likely to slow or reverse.

whyNot.0: This continues the old trend while ignoring the stated cause that is ending.
whyNot.2: New employers are never mentioned; this needs an unstated event.
whyNot.3: Nothing supports faster growth, let alone doubling, once the plant closes.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Nurse Ahmed Saleh has a reputation on his unit for patience. He explains each medication slowly, draws diagrams for patients who seem confused and stays after his shift to answer families' questions. A new patient, Mr. Lyle, tells Ahmed that he does not understand his discharge instructions.

Based on the passage, how will Ahmed most likely respond?
options: He will refer Mr. Lyle to a pharmacist for an explanation.
He will tell Mr. Lyle to read the instructions again at home.
He will go over the instructions slowly, using a diagram.
He will ask Mr. Lyle's family to explain them instead.
B.why: Ahmed's established traits are patience, slow explanation and drawing diagrams for confused patients. Applying those traits to the new situation gives the most likely response.

whyNot.0: Referring the patient away does not fit his habit of explaining things himself.
whyNot.1: Sending the patient home to reread contradicts his patient, hands-on approach.
whyNot.3: The passage shows him answering families' questions, not handing his job to them.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Sales of paper planners at Corner Books fell each year from 2019 to 2022. In 2023, a popular video series about 'screen-free organizing' spread online, and the store's planner sales rose for the first time in five years. The store manager has ordered twice as many planners for next year, and the video's creator has announced a second series.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
options: Planner sales will likely rise again next year.
Planner sales will likely fall as they did before.
Planner sales will likely double at most stores.
Planner sales will likely depend on store prices.
C.why: The long decline reversed in 2023 for a stated reason, the video series, and that cause continues with a second series. With the manager stocking more, a further rise is the best-supported prediction.

whyNot.1: Going back to the old decline ignores the new cause that reversed it.
whyNot.2: Doubling at most stores overreaches: the text covers one store, and doubled orders are not doubled sales.
whyNot.3: Prices are never discussed, so this prediction has no basis in the text.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The Westside Health Fair has been held in the high school gym every October for ten years. Attendance has grown each year, and last year the gym was so full that some visitors waited outside for an hour. Organizers have reserved the larger convention center for this October.

If added to the passage, which detail would make the prediction 'Attendance will grow again this year' LESS likely?
options: The convention center holds about twice as many people.
The local newspaper will advertise the fair for a month.
This year's fair falls on the same day as a large festival.
Several new clinics have signed up to offer free screenings.
C.why: A competing large event on the same day introduces a cause that could pull visitors away, weakening the prediction of continued growth.

whyNot.0: More space removes last year's limit, which makes growth more likely.
whyNot.1: Advertising tends to raise attendance, supporting the prediction.
whyNot.3: More free screenings give visitors more reasons to come, supporting growth.

C.q:
Read the passage.

When Keisha joined the hospital's volunteer program, she asked to work in the gift shop because she disliked crowds. Within a month she had reorganized the shelves, built a simple inventory sheet and suggested a new layout that the manager adopted. Next week, the volunteer coordinator will ask for a helper to sort the hospital's donated books in a quiet storage room.

Based on the passage, which prediction about Keisha is best supported?
options: She will turn down the task because she prefers the gift shop.
She will be chosen to lead the volunteer program next month.
She will ask to greet visitors at the main entrance instead.
She will volunteer to sort and organize the donated books.
C.why: Keisha prefers quiet work away from crowds and has shown a talent for organizing. A sorting job in a quiet room fits both traits.

whyNot.0: She chose the gift shop to avoid crowds, not out of loyalty to it; a quiet room suits her too.
whyNot.1: A leadership role is an unstated event with no hint in the passage.
whyNot.2: Greeting visitors at a busy entrance conflicts with her dislike of crowds.

reteach.title: Think of a weather forecast
reteach.question: A forecaster says, 'Rain by evening.' She did not guess: she read the clouds, the wind and the radar. How is that like predicting from a passage?

blocks.body: A forecaster looks at what is already happening (clouds building, wind shifting) and projects it forward. She would never forecast snow in July because she wishes it would snow, and she changes her forecast only when the data changes. Do the same with a passage: find what is already moving, project it one step forward, and change direction only when the text gives you a new cause.

steps.label: Observe
steps.sub: Pattern, trait or trend in the text

blocks.text: A forecast of 'heavy rain everywhere forever' is not bold, it is wrong. Predictions with all, every or forever usually overreach what the text supports.

explain.body: A prediction states what is likely to happen next or in a new situation. It must grow out of evidence in the text: a pattern, a trait, a trend, a cause in motion or a hint the author planted.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The pediatric clinic's flu shot clinics have filled up faster each fall for four years. This year, the county added a rule that children must have a flu shot to attend public preschool.

Which prediction is best supported?
options: Demand for the clinic's flu shots will likely rise this fall.
Fewer parents will likely bring children for flu shots this fall.
The county will likely end the preschool rule within a year.
Every child in the county will likely get a shot from the clinic.
test.why: Demand has grown four years running, and the new preschool rule adds another reason to get a shot. Both clues point to rising demand.

whyNot.1: This reverses a steady trend with no cause; the new rule pushes the other way.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the county plans to drop the rule.
whyNot.3: Overreach: other providers may give shots, and 'every child' goes beyond the text.

explain.body: If something has happened the same way several times, or numbers have moved steadily one way, the text expects that to continue. A trend changes direction only when the text gives a cause, such as a closure, a new rule or a new competitor.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The Harbor Café has run a 'pay what you can' night on the last Friday of each month for a year. Each month, more diners have come, and the café has covered its costs every time. The owner says nothing about the program will change.

Which prediction is best supported for next month's event?
options: The café will end the program because it loses money.
Attendance will drop as diners lose interest in the idea.
The café will hold the event and likely cover its costs.
The café will move the event to a bigger dining room.
test.why: The pattern is steady: monthly events, growing attendance, costs covered, and no planned changes. Continuing that pattern is the best-supported prediction.

whyNot.0: The text says the café covers its costs, so this contradicts the passage.
whyNot.1: Attendance has grown every month; a drop has no stated cause.
whyNot.3: A new room is an unstated event; the owner says nothing will change.

explain.body: In stories, people keep acting in character: a careful person stays careful, an impulsive one acts fast. Authors also plant hints early (a blinking warning light, a frayed rope) that point to a later event.

test.q:
Read the passage.

Before every road trip, Marcus checks the tire pressure, tops up the oil and packs a first-aid kit. On the morning of a long drive to his cousin's wedding, he notices one tire looks slightly flat.

What is Marcus most likely to do?
options: Drive to the wedding and check the tire when he arrives.
Cancel the trip and send his cousin a gift by mail.
Ask his cousin to pick him up for the long drive.
Check and fix the tire before setting out on the drive.
test.why: Marcus's trait is careful preparation before trips. A low tire fits his routine of checking pressure, so he will most likely deal with it before he leaves.

whyNot.0: Driving on a suspect tire goes against his careful habits.
whyNot.1: Canceling is a large leap; the problem is small and fixable.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests he would hand off the trip; he prepares to drive himself.

explain.body: Reject a prediction if it needs an event the text never mentions, reverses a trend with no stated cause, rests on outside knowledge or uses absolute words (all, every, never) the evidence cannot carry.

test.q:
Read the passage.

The community pool's swim lessons have sold out within a day each spring for three years. This spring, the pool added two more instructors, which lets it offer twice as many lessons.

Which prediction is LEAST supported by the passage?
options: More children will be able to take lessons this spring.
Lessons will likely fill up more slowly than in past years.
The pool will cancel lessons because too few people sign up.
The new instructors will likely teach some of the lessons.
test.why: Lessons have sold out within a day for three years. Predicting cancellation for low sign-ups reverses that pattern with no cause in the text.

whyNot.0: Twice as many lessons means more spots, so this is well supported.
whyNot.1: With double the spots, selling out may take longer; this follows from the added capacity.
whyNot.3: The instructors were added to offer more lessons, so they will likely teach them.
